title: Step 8: Connect Zotero
text:
Due by Friday, 25 September 2026
With this step the agent can search your Zotero library, read the PDFs in it, and pull citation keys while it writes. The connection is a small program called zotero-mcp that talks to Zotero on your own computer, through the local access you switched on in step 7. It reads your library and does not change it.
Zotero has to be running whenever the agent uses it.

title: Step 8: Connect Zotero
text:
Part 1: Install
zotero-mcp is a Python program. The installer below, called uv, takes care of Python for you.

macOSWindows


Open the Terminal app (any folder is fine), copy the line below, paste it after the prompt, and press Enter. It prints where uv was installed:
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh


Open PowerShell, copy the line below, paste it after the prompt, and press Enter:
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"



Close the terminal and open a new one, so the new installer is found. Then install the program, in the terminal:
uv tool install zotero-mcp-server
Check, in the same terminal. It prints a version number:
zotero-mcp version

title: Step 8: Connect Zotero
section: Part 2: Register it with Claude Code
text:
Part 2: Register it with Claude Code
Open a terminal (any folder is fine, the setting is not tied to a folder), copy this line, paste it after the prompt, and press Enter:
claude mcp add -s user zotero -e ZOTERO_LOCAL=true -- zotero-mcp
It answers with a line saying the server was added. Then, with the Zotero app running, check:
claude mcp list
The zotero line should end in Connected. If it says it failed to connect, the two usual causes are that Zotero is not running, or that the setting from step 7 (Settings, Advanced, Allow other applications on this computer to communicate with Zotero) is not ticked. On Windows there is a third: a terminal opened before the install in Part 1 finished does not find zotero-mcp. Open a new one and check again.

title: Step 8: Connect Zotero
text:
Part 3: Try it
Keep Zotero open. Open a terminal at your setup repository (as in step 4), start claude, and ask something your library can answer, for example:

Which items in my Zotero library are about sanitation?

If Claude Code asks before using the zotero tool, read the prompt and allow it; in auto mode it runs without asking. The answer lists items from your own library, with titles and citation keys. If it answers that it cannot reach Zotero, the app is not running or the Advanced setting from step 7 is off; fix that and ask again.






NoteWhat you do not need



The zotero-mcp project offers extras for semantic search and PDF page images. The base install is enough for the workshop. Leave the extras out.

title: Step 6: Connect your R session
text:
Due by Friday, 25 September 2026
Claude Code has no R session of its own. It can run a script or render a Quarto document, but it cannot see the data frame you have open in RStudio. The mcptools package changes that. It lets the agent run R code inside your running RStudio session and look at the objects there, which is how it inspects your data on the day. This connection is specific to R and RStudio, see the note on the Prepare page. If you work in another language or editor, the agent still works, but this step may not apply.

title: Step 6: Connect your R session
text:
Part 1: Install the package
Open RStudio. The Console is the pane at the bottom left, the one with a > prompt. Click into it, type the line below, and press Enter. Wait until the download messages stop and the prompt is back:
install.packages("mcptools")

title: Step 6: Connect your R session
section: Part 2: Register it with Claude Code
text:
Part 2: Register it with Claude Code

macOSWindows


Open the Terminal app (Spotlight, then type Terminal). Any folder is fine, this setting is not tied to a folder. Copy the line below, paste it after the prompt, and press Enter. It answers with a line saying the server was added:
claude mcp add -s user r-mcptools -- Rscript -e "mcptools::mcp_server()"


Open PowerShell (Start menu, then type PowerShell). On Windows the Rscript program is usually not findable from the terminal, so you give the full path. Get it from the RStudio Console, the pane at the bottom left:
normalizePath(file.path(R.home("bin"), "Rscript.exe"))
It prints something like C:\Program Files\R\R-4.5.1\bin\Rscript.exe. Use your path, in quotes, in PowerShell:
claude mcp add -s user r-mcptools -- "C:\Program Files\R\R-4.5.1\bin\Rscript.exe" -e "mcptools::mcp_server()"



Check, in the same terminal:
claude mcp list
The line for r-mcptools should end in Connected.

title: Step 6: Connect your R session
section: Part 3: Let R announce its sessions
text:
Part 3: Let R announce its sessions
The server needs to know which R session to talk to. One line in your R profile registers every RStudio session you start.
Back in RStudio, click into the Console and run:
file.edit("~/.Rprofile")
A file called .Rprofile opens in the editor pane at the top left. It is empty unless you have set up R this way before. Paste this line into it, then save with Cmd+S on macOS or Ctrl+S on Windows:
if (interactive()) mcptools::mcp_session()
Restart R from the menu bar: Session, Restart R. The Console clears and shows a fresh prompt. Then, in the Console, create something for the agent to look at:
x <- head(mtcars)

title: Step 6: Connect your R session
text:
Part 4: Try it
Check the Environment pane at the top right of RStudio: x is listed there as 6 obs. of 11 variables. Now open a terminal at your setup repository (as in step 4), start claude, and ask:

What objects are in my R session?

If Claude Code asks before using the r-mcptools tool, read the prompt and allow it; in auto mode it runs without asking. The answer names x and describes it as a data frame with 6 rows and 11 columns. On the day you do the same with the workshop data loaded.






ImportantWhat this connection means



With this in place the agent can run any R code in your live session, including code that removes objects or writes files. In manual mode the permission prompt is what stands between it and that; in auto mode a built-in check takes that role, and it does not know your data. Read what the agent proposes, or what it did, rather than approving by reflex. That habit is the point of the workshop, and this is where you start it.

title: Step 4: Install Claude Code and log in
text:
Due by Friday, 25 September 2026
Claude Code is the coding agent we use on the day. It runs in a terminal, works inside the folder you start it in, reads and edits files there, and runs commands. It asks before it runs a command or changes a file, and that permission prompt is the first thing to learn to read.
This step has three parts: get an account, install the program, and log in once from a small repository I prepared for you.

title: Step 4: Install Claude Code and log in
text:
Part 1: Your Claude account
Claude Code is not part of the free Claude plan. You need one of the two routes below.

GHE membersEveryone else


You will receive an email invitation to the Global Health Engineering organization on the Claude Team plan, sent to your ETH email address. Accept it. If you do not have a Claude account under that address yet, the invitation walks you through creating one.
Use your ETH address, not a personal one. If you already use Claude with a personal address, the Team seat is a separate account and you log into Claude Code with the ETH one.
The invitation expires after three weeks. If none has arrived by the time you reach this step, tell me in the chat room.
On the Team plan, what you type and what the agent reads is not used to train models, and the group, not the vendor, controls the data. That is the reason for the plan.


Create your own account at claude.ai and subscribe to a paid plan for the month of the workshop. The Pro plan is enough. I suggest the Max plan for one month, since the day involves a lot of agent work and the Pro limits can run out in an afternoon. Cancel afterwards if you do not want to keep it.
Then do one thing before anything else: open your privacy settings and turn off the setting that allows your chats and coding sessions to be used for model training. On the Free, Pro and Max plans that setting is on unless you turn it off, and it covers Claude Code sessions. With the setting off, your data is kept for 30 days instead of five years and is not used for training.

title: Step 4: Install Claude Code and log in
text:
Part 2: Install
The installer needs nothing else on your computer. Open a terminal and paste one line.

macOSWindows


Open Terminal (in Applications, Utilities, or search for it with Spotlight) and run:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash


Open PowerShell (search for it in the Start menu) and run:
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex
Claude Code uses Git for Windows, which you installed for the first workshop, to run commands. If you skipped that step then, install it from git-scm.com first.



Close the terminal and open a new one, so it picks up the new program. Then check the install:
claude --version
claude doctor
The first prints a version number. The second checks the installation and prints what it found. Both should finish without an error.






TipWhich terminal



Any terminal works, including the Terminal tab in RStudio (Tools, Terminal, New Terminal). On the Mac, iTerm is a good alternative to the built-in Terminal; if you are interested in using it, get in touch. On Windows, run the two install lines above in PowerShell, and use whichever terminal you like afterwards.

title: Step 4: Install Claude Code and log in
section: Part 3: Clone your setup repository and log in
text:
Part 3: Clone your setup repository and log in

Clone your setup repository
I have created a repository for you in the organization, named setup-USERNAME with your GitHub username in place of USERNAME. It holds a small public dataset and one R script, and it is where every test before the day runs.

Open the organization page, https://github.com/agentsforsci-ghe/, and find setup-USERNAME in the list of repositories. Use the search field on that page if the list is long.
Open it, click the green Code button, and copy the HTTPS URL.
In RStudio, choose File, New Project, Version Control, Git, paste the URL, pick where the folder should live, and click Create Project. This is the same clone you did in the first workshop; the instructions from then still apply, screenshots included.

RStudio opens the new project. The Files pane at the bottom right shows 01-read-data.R, a data folder, and a README.






ImportantNo repository with your name



Tell me in the chat room. Creating it takes me a minute.




Open a terminal at that folder
Claude Code works in the folder you start it from, so the terminal has to be opened inside the setup repository. I like to open a terminal separately from RStudio while working on a project, and keep the two windows next to each other, filling the screen. RStudio and other editors also have a terminal built in. Both ways are described below. Pick one and try out what works for you.

RStudiomacOS FinderWindows Explorer


With the project open, choose Tools, Terminal, New Terminal. A Terminal tab appears next to the Console, already inside the project folder. This works the same on macOS and Windows.


Open Finder and go to the folder you just created, for example Documents/setup-USERNAME. Right-click the folder and choose New Terminal at Folder. A Terminal window opens inside it. If the entry is missing from the menu, look under Services in the same menu, or switch it on once under System Settings, Keyboard, Keyboard Shortcuts, Services, Files and Folders.


Open File Explorer and open the folder you just created. Right-click an empty area inside the folder and choose Open in Terminal. On Windows 10, hold Shift while right-clicking and choose Open PowerShell window here. Open Git Bash here, which Git for Windows added to the same menu, works as well.



Whichever way you chose, the prompt in the terminal ends with the folder name, setup-USERNAME. If it does not, you are in the wrong folder.


Log in

In that terminal, start Claude Code:
claude
The first start asks you to pick a colour theme, then opens your browser to log in. Log in with the account from Part 1. If the browser does not open, press c to copy the login link and paste it into a browser yourself. GHE members: if asked which organization to use, pick Global Health Engineering.
Back in the terminal, type /status and press Enter. It shows which account you are logged in with. Check that it is the one you intended.
Look at the bottom line of the window, where Claude Code shows its permission mode. On the Team, Pro and Max plans it starts in auto mode: a built-in check approves ordinary actions on its own and asks you only when something looks risky. Pressing Shift+Tab switches to manual mode, where it asks before every command. Either is fine for the pre-work. On the workshop day we work in auto mode.
Say hello. Type a greeting and press Enter. You get a greeting back. That is the whole test.
Type /exit to leave.

Do not ask it to do anything else yet. Step 9 is where you give it work, with the safety rails in place.






NoteWhy a setup repository and not your own



The agent reads whole folders and sends what it finds to a model. Before the day, it does not see the data you committed in step 1. Every test in steps 4 to 9 runs in setup-USERNAME, which holds public data prepared for exactly this. We set the safety rails for your own repository together in the room.








ImportantIf the login fails on the ETH network



Claude Code needs to reach a handful of addresses (claude.ai, api.anthropic.com, platform.claude.com and downloads.claude.ai). If the login page never opens or the terminal reports a connection error while you are on eduroam or the ETH network, try again on a phone hotspot and tell me in the chat room which network failed.








NoteIf the install fails



Claude Code also exists as a website, claude.ai/code, that works from your GitHub repository without anything on your laptop. It is the fallback for the day if the local install cannot be fixed. Tell me before the workshop so we can set it up together.

title: Step 1: Create your repository and add your data
text:
Due by Monday, 14 September 2026
Everything here uses the Git and GitHub workflow from Git for Scientists. If a step is unfamiliar, the instructions from that workshop still apply. If you are would like support in completing a step, please reach out to the course instructor.

title: Step 1: Create your repository and add your data
section: Accept the invitation to the organization
text:
Accept the invitation to the organization
You have been invited to the agentsforsci-ghe organization on GitHub. Accept the invitation before you start working on the tasks below.
The invitation arrived by email. You can also accept it by going to https://github.com/agentsforsci-ghe/ while signed in to GitHub, where a banner offers you the invitation.






NoteCheck the right inbox



GitHub sent the invitation to the email address you used to register your GitHub account. That is not necessarily your institutional email address. If nothing has arrived, check the other address you might have signed up with, and look in the spam folder.
You can see which address GitHub has for you under Settings, Emails.

title: Step 1: Create your repository and add your data
text:
Create the repository
Once you are a member, create a new repository in the agentsforsci-ghe organization.
The name should broadly reflect what you work with, following three rules:

lowercase letters only
at most two words
words separated by a dash

For example: solidwaste-kampala.
Two settings to choose on the same screen:

Visibility: public if you can, private if you cannot
Initialise this repository with: tick Add a README file

Visibility. Choose public if the data allows it. The aim is for every repository to be public by the end, so the work and its outcomes can be shown to others. If you are not ready to make yours public yet, start private and switch it later under Settings. What you must not do is treat private as permission to commit something sensitive: the rule below applies either way.
README. Ticking Add a README file means GitHub creates the repository with a file already in it, so you can clone it straight away. Without it you get an empty repository and a set of setup commands instead.

title: Step 1: Create your repository and add your data
text:
Clone it
Clone the repository to your computer, the same way you did in the first workshop.
If you would like to walk through it again, the instructions are still online: cloning a repository.

title: Step 1: Create your repository and add your data
text:
Add a folder called data
Inside your cloned repository, create a folder named data, and put the dataset you plan to work with into it.
What to bring. Something real from your own research, small enough to look at in one sitting. Several files are okay with a few hundred to a few thousand rows and columns you can explain. It does not need to be tidy or finished. Messy real data could be very useful here. Any file format is okay: CSV or XLSX, also PDF and DOCX, or JSON, etc.






ImportantThis must be non-sensitive data, with no personal data in it



Personal and sensitive data never go into a Git repository, private repositories included. Git history is permanent, and a later visibility change, a new collaborator, or a push to the wrong remote can expose it.
Do not commit names, recruitment or participant data, health data, signed consent, or anything that identifies a person in combination with other columns.
This matters more with an agent than without one: a coding agent reads whole directories and sends file contents to a model, so protected data in the folder can leave your machine without you deciding to send it.
If you are unsure which category your data falls into, treat it as protected and ask before committing anything.








NoteIf you cannot identify a dataset



Get in touch with me directly and we will sort something out before the workshop. Do not skip the step and turn up without data.

title: Step 1: Create your repository and add your data
text:
Commit and push
Stage the data, commit it with a clear message, and push to GitHub. Then open your repository in the browser and check the file is actually there.

title: Step 1: Create your repository and add your data
text:
Open an issue
Once the data is committed and pushed, open an issue on your own repository:

Title: Data added
Body: one or two sentences saying what the data is and where it came from
Assignee: larnsce

That issue is how I know you are ready, and the description is the beginning of the documentation question we work on during the day.






ImportantAll of this by Monday, 14 September 2026



If anything blocks you, open the issue anyway, describe what went wrong, and assign it to me. A problem found now is half an hour of work; the same problem found on the morning of the workshop costs you the session.

title: Agents for Scientists
text:
Thank you for joining this workshop. Your course instructor Lars Schöbitz is looking forward to meeting you.
We will meet on Tuesday, 29 September 2026 - 08:30 to 17:00 (Europe/Zurich) at Villa Hatt, ETH Zurich.
This is the second of the two workshops in the series. The first, Git for Scientists, ran on 15 July 2026 and is the foundation this day builds on.

title: Agents for Scientists
text:
Background
In the first workshop you learned to use Git and GitHub so that every change to a project is versioned, documented, and open to review. This workshop puts a coding agent inside that same workflow.
The day runs the real work of writing a paper (analysing data, preparing a literature review, publishing a manuscript) under three conditions: as you do it now without agents, with an agent given minimal input, and with an agent given a proper plan and using GitHub issues. Comparing the three shows what the agent actually does for you, how you can document the process and how your stay involved in making decisions.
Because the work runs through Git and GitHub, every action an agent takes and every decision you make is recorded as you go. That record is what makes agent use traceable and declarable, which is the second half of the day: research integrity bodies are writing disclosure rules for scientific research right now, and we are planning to use to send them a response written from what we do in the room.

title: Agents for Scientists
text:
Prior knowledge
Everyone taking part has been through the Git for Scientists workshop, so this builds directly on it. You should be able to:

clone a repository and open it as a project
run the pull, stage, commit, push cycle
create a branch and open a pull request
review a colleague’s pull request and merge it
open an issue, assign it, and close it

If any of these are shaky, work through the Git for Scientists material again before the day. You do not need any prior experience with AI coding agents.

title: Agents for Scientists
text:
Learning objectives






NoteTentative



These objectives are still under active development and will be refined before the workshop.


By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

Run an agent inside the Git workflow: give a coding agent a task, write its plan down as GitHub issues before any code is produced, then review what it produced as a pull request and accept or reject the change.
Judge the difference a plan makes: compare the output of an agent given minimal input against one given a reviewed plan, and say what changed and why.
Judge the difference documentation makes: compare what an agent does with a plain CSV against the same data published as a data package.
Declare agent use: point to the record your workflow produced and say what it shows about which parts of the work an agent touched.

title: Step 5: Connect GitHub
text:
Due by Friday, 25 September 2026
On the day, the agent opens issues and pull requests on your repository for you. For that it needs to talk to GitHub from the terminal, which the GitHub CLI provides. Two parts: install the GitHub CLI and log in, then create a dev branch.

title: Step 5: Connect GitHub
text:
Part 1: The GitHub CLI

macOSWindows


The GitHub CLI comes through Homebrew, the package manager for the Mac. If you do not have Homebrew yet, go to brew.sh, copy the install line shown at the top of that page, paste it into Terminal, press Enter, and follow the prompts. It asks for your Mac password and takes a few minutes. Then, in the same Terminal window, install the GitHub CLI:
brew install gh


Open PowerShell (as in step 4), paste this line, and press Enter:
winget install --id GitHub.cli --source winget
Close the terminal and open a new window afterwards, so the new program is found.



Now connect the CLI to your GitHub account. In the terminal, run:
gh auth login
It asks a few questions. Answer GitHub.com, HTTPS, Yes to authenticating Git with your GitHub credentials, and Login with a web browser. Copy the one-time code it shows, press Enter, paste the code into the browser page that opens, and authorize.
Check it worked:
gh auth status
Then open a terminal at your setup repository (as in step 4) and run one command that only works when GitHub is reachable:
gh repo view
It prints the name and README of setup-USERNAME.






NoteThe token from the first workshop



The personal access token you created for the first workshop keeps working for RStudio. The GitHub CLI has its own login, which is what you just did. The two do not interfere.

title: Step 5: Connect GitHub
text:
Part 2: A dev branch
The working pattern for the day is that changes land on a branch called dev, get reviewed in a pull request, and reach main through the merge. Create the branch now so it is there when the agent starts working.
Create it on your own repository from step 1, the one with your data, which is where the day’s work happens. Open that project in RStudio with File, Open Project.
In the Git pane, click the New Branch button. Name it dev, leave Sync branch with remote ticked, and click Create. RStudio creates the branch, switches to it, and pushes it to GitHub.
Check on GitHub: the branch menu on your repository page now lists main and dev.






NoteNot using RStudio



Create a branch called dev and push it with whatever tool you prefer. The name is what matters.








NoteAnnounced for the day: two GHE skills



During the workshop we install two small skills written at Global Health Engineering, one that turns the agent’s changes into a commit with a record of what the agent did, and one that opens a pull request from dev into main. They are installed in Claude Code with two commands, take a minute, and can be removed again after the day. Nothing to do now. If you are curious, they live at Global-Health-Engineering/skills.

title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
text:
Due by Friday, 25 September 2026
One of the three paper tasks on the day is a literature review, and the agent does it against your own reference library. This page sets up Zotero, the free and open source reference manager, the way we use it in the group. If you already use Zotero, skim to Step 5 and check the settings from there on. The citation key settings in Step 7 are the group convention and are worth checking even on a library you have used for years.
Written against Zotero 10 (10.0.3, September 2026), which came out in August, and the current Better BibTeX release. If you run an older Zotero, update it first. Two things differ from older guides you may find online: the Sync tab in the settings is now called Account, and Better BibTeX runs on Zotero 10 even though its release notes still name older versions.

title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
text:
What you are setting up

Zotero, the desktop app. It stores your references, the PDFs attached to them, and your reading highlights.
A zotero.org account with sync, so your library is backed up and available on other devices.
The Zotero Connector, a browser extension that saves papers into your library with one click.
Better BibTeX, a Zotero plugin that gives every item a stable short ID called a citation key, for example forte2022building. Citation keys are how Quarto, LaTeX and other plain text tools refer to items.
Two settings inside Zotero: local access for other apps on your computer, which step 8 depends on, and Quick Copy, which puts a citation key on your clipboard with one keystroke.

title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
text:
Step 1: Install Zotero

Go to zotero.org/download.
Download the installer for your platform and install it like any other app.
Open Zotero once so it can create its data folder.

If Zotero is already installed, update it before you continue. On macOS use Zotero, Check for Updates. On Windows use Help, Check for Updates. The steps below were checked on Zotero 10 and need Zotero 7 or newer.
Throughout this page, “Settings” means the window you open with Zotero, Settings on macOS or Edit, Settings on Windows.

title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
section: Step 2: Create an account and turn on sync
text:
Step 2: Create an account and turn on sync

Create a free account at zotero.org/user/register and confirm the email it sends you.
In Zotero, open Settings, Account (older versions call this tab Sync).
Sign in with your new account.
Leave the data syncing defaults as they are. Data syncing covers your references, notes, tags and highlights. It is free and has no size limit.

File syncing is a separate switch on the same tab and covers the PDFs themselves. Every account gets 300 MB of file storage for free. Keep it on with the “Zotero” option if you want to read your PDFs on a second device; decide about paid storage later if the library outgrows the free tier.

title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
text:
Step 3: Install the browser connector

In the browser you normally use, go to zotero.org/download. The page detects your browser and offers the matching connector.
Install the extension and pin its button to the toolbar.
Keep the Zotero desktop app open while you save. The connector hands items to the desktop app.

To save an item, open the paper’s page (the journal landing page, an arXiv abstract page) and click the connector button. Zotero saves the reference and, when it has access, the PDF.
Two other ways to add items, both inside Zotero: click the magic wand button and paste a DOI, ISBN, PMID or arXiv ID, or drag a PDF file into the Zotero window and check the metadata it reads out of it.

title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
section: Step 4: Know your way around the library
text:
Step 4: Know your way around the library
If you have used a reference manager before, skim this. If Zotero is your first one, ten minutes here pay off.

The left pane lists your collections. A collection is a folder you assign items to. One item can sit in several collections at once.
The middle pane lists the items in the selected collection. An item is the reference record: title, authors, year, journal, DOI.
Attachments (the PDF), notes and tags hang off an item. Click the arrow next to an item to see them.
The right pane shows the selected item’s fields. Fix obvious metadata errors as you notice them, because everything downstream builds on these fields.
Double-click an item to open its PDF in Zotero’s reader. Highlights are stored in Zotero’s database and sync like any other data.

Save two or three real papers now so you have something to test with.

title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
section: Step 5: Allow other apps to talk to Zotero
text:
Step 5: Allow other apps to talk to Zotero
Step 8 connects the agent to your library through a local connection on your own computer. One checkbox enables it.

Open Settings, Advanced.
Check Allow other applications on this computer to communicate with Zotero.

The connection only works for apps running on the same computer. Nothing is exposed to the internet.

title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
text:
Step 6: Install Better BibTeX
Better BibTeX is installed from a downloaded file.

In your browser, go to the Better BibTeX releases page and download the latest .xpi file. You want the file saved to disk, not opened by the browser.

SafariFirefoxChrome and Edge


Click the .xpi link. Safari downloads it to your Downloads folder. If it opens a viewer instead, right-click the link and choose Download Linked File.


Firefox tries to install .xpi files as Firefox extensions, which is the wrong target. Right-click the link and choose Save Link As.


Click the link. If the browser warns that the file may be dangerous because it is an uncommon type, choose Keep. The file is safe.



In Zotero, go to Tools, Plugins.
Click the gear icon, choose Install Plugin From File, and select the .xpi you downloaded.
Restart Zotero when prompted.

After the restart, the Settings window has a new Better BibTeX tab.

title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
text:
Step 7: Configure the citation keys
This is the step to get exactly right.
A citation key is a short, readable ID for one item, like forte2022building. Once other tools refer to your items by these keys, a key must never change. When everyone in a group generates keys the same way, a paper shared through a group library carries the same key in every member’s library, and drafts move between people without anyone rekeying citations. The formula below is the shared convention at Global Health Engineering.
Open Settings, Better BibTeX. Under Citation keys:

Set the citation key formula to:
auth.lower + year + veryshorttitle(1, 0).lower
Read left to right: the last name of the first author, lowercased; the publication year; the first meaningful word of the title, lowercased. Tiago Forte’s 2022 book “Building a Second Brain” gets the key forte2022building.
Set Automatically fill citation key after to 2 seconds. Filling writes the generated key into the item’s own Citation Key field, where it is saved and synced.
Check that Regenerate citation key when item changes is unchecked. With it unchecked, a filled key stays as it is even when you later fix a typo in the author or title, which is what you want. If it is checked, uncheck it now.

Leave the remaining defaults. Then add a Citation Key column to your item list: right-click the column header in the middle pane and tick Citation Key.
Items that were already in your library may carry keys from the old default formula. Select them, right-click, and choose Better BibTeX, Regenerate citation key. Do this now, before anything refers to the old keys.

title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
text:
Step 8: Set up Quick Copy

Open Settings, Export.
Under Quick Copy, set Item Format to Better BibTeX Citation Key Quick Copy.
Check that Note Format is Markdown + Rich Text and that Include Zotero Links is ticked on the Markdown line.

From now on, selecting an item and pressing Cmd+Shift+C on macOS or Ctrl+Shift+C on Windows copies its citation key.

title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
text:
Check
Save one more paper with the connector. Within two seconds its right pane shows a Citation Key in the shape authorYEARword. Select it, press the Quick Copy shortcut, paste into any text editor, and you get the bare key. Edit the title, wait two seconds, and confirm the key did not change. If all three worked, the setup is complete, and step 8 connects it to the agent.






NoteWhere this page comes from



Adapted from the Zotero getting-started guide written for the Global Health Engineering group in July 2026, shortened to what the workshop needs and checked against Zotero 10 in September 2026.

title: Step 9: Test your setup and report done
text:
Due by Friday, 25 September 2026
Twenty minutes. This runs everything from steps 4 to 8 once, in the order the day uses it, on the setup repository you cloned in step 4, and ends with an issue assigned to me so I know you are ready. Have Zotero open, and RStudio open with the setup project (File, Open Project, then setup.Rproj in the folder you cloned).

title: Step 9: Test your setup and report done
text:
1. Both connections
In RStudio, open a terminal inside the project: Tools, Terminal, New Terminal. A Terminal tab appears next to the Console, already in the setup folder. Run:
claude mcp list
Both r-mcptools and zotero end in Connected. If one does not, go back to step 6 or step 8 before continuing.

title: Step 9: Test your setup and report done
section: 2. Put the data in your R session
text:
2. Put the data in your R session
In the Files pane at the bottom right, click 01-read-data.R to open it, then click Source at the top right of the editor. There is nothing to edit. The Console prints a line starting with “Loaded”, and the Environment pane at the top right lists two objects, investments and investments_by_country.

title: Step 9: Test your setup and report done
section: 3. A read-only run in plan mode
text:
3. A read-only run in plan mode
In the Terminal tab, start Claude Code:
claude
Press Shift+Tab until the status line at the bottom says plan mode. In plan mode the agent reads and proposes. It does not change anything. Ask these three things, one at a time, and wait for each answer:

Read the files in the data folder and describe what is in them. Do not change anything.


What objects are in my R session, and how many rows does the largest one have?


List five items from my Zotero library with their citation keys.

When Claude Code asks before using a tool, read the prompt and allow it. In auto mode most of these steps run without asking, and each answer names the tool it used. The three answers show the agent reading the sample data, your R session, and your own library.






NoteIf it proposes something you did not ask for



Say no. In plan mode the agent may only read. Anything else is a good story for the chat room.

title: Step 9: Test your setup and report done
text:
4. A file and a commit
Press Shift+Tab to leave plan mode. Ask:

Create a file called SETUP.md at the top of this repository. In it, list my operating system, the Claude Code version, whether the r-mcptools and zotero servers are connected, and a short summary of what is in the data folder. Do not run git.

The agent shows the file it wants to write. Read it and accept. Then type /exit.
Commit and push the file yourself, the way you did in the first workshop: in the RStudio Git pane, tick SETUP.md to stage it, click Commit, write “Add setup report” as the message, click Commit, then Push. Open the repository on GitHub and check that SETUP.md is there.
Today you do every commit yourself. On the day you hand the agent one step at a time.

title: Step 9: Test your setup and report done
text:
5. Report done
Open an issue on your setup repository with the title Setup complete, assigned to larnsce, saying which of the steps 4 to 9 worked and which did not. You can have the agent do it. Start claude again in the Terminal tab and ask:

Open an issue on this repository titled “Setup complete”, assign it to larnsce, and write in the body which of the pre-work steps 4 to 9 worked for me and which did not.

It uses the GitHub CLI from step 5 for that. Allow the prompt if one appears, and check on GitHub that the issue exists. Opening the issue by hand, as you did in step 1, is just as good.






ImportantIf anything failed



Open the issue anyway, describe what failed and at which step, and assign it to me. A problem found now is half an hour of work. The same problem found on the morning of the workshop costs you the session.


Thank you for working through all of this. See you at Villa Hatt, ETH Zurich.
